newsitem.title: UK: Polish c.bank chief seeks single-digit CPI.
newsitem.headline: Polish c.bank chief seeks single-digit CPI.

text.p: Polish central bank President Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz, who took office with inflation at 60 percent, said on Tuesday she hoped to complete her term next year with the rate in single digits.

In an interview with Reuters, she also said it was not good enough for the government to keep the growing budget deficit within western Europe's Maastricht Treaty criteria, and ruled out an immediate interest rate cut due to soaring lending.

Gronkiewicz-Waltz has won praise from the West for her tireless battle against inflation since she was appointed in 1992. But the tough monetary medicine she has administered has made her unpopular in Poland and she admitted that her prospects for another term at the National Bank of Poland were uncertain.

Poland, which was in economic crisis when the communists fell in 1989, imposed several years of shock therapy which sent unemployment soaring but has turned the country into one of Europe's fastest-growing economies.
Inflation remains high by western standards but has fallen sharply under Gronkiewicz-Waltz.

Finance Minister Marek Belka said this week he hoped annual inflation could be cut to 13 percent by the end of this year and into single digits by 1998. In March, inflation was 16.6 percent compared with 20.4 percent a year earlier.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz, in London for the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, declined to forecast a fall into single figures in 1998.

But she added: "I would like to (achieve this) because it's the last year of my term. When I came to the bank I said that I hoped I would leave the bank with single-digit inflation. I came when it was about 60 percent a year."
The reformist governments based around Solidarity trade union won few friends at home for the shock treatment after 1989 and reformed communists and their allies won power in 1993.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz said her role in cutting inflation had also carried a price. "I am quite credible but I'm not sure if I'm quite popular," she said.
Her term expires on March 5, 1998. To win a second term, she needs to be put forward by President Aleksander Kwasniewski, a former communist, and then approved by parliament.
Asked about her chances of winning a second term, she said: "From the legal point of view it's possible, but I think it will be difficult because I kept quite tough monetary policies."
In her latest battle with politicians, she is trying to preserve the National Bank's power to supervise banks and decide monetary policy under a draft banking law.
Members of parliament have produced a plan giving greater political control and limiting the central bank's independence.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz, who ran unsuccessfully for the presidency in the last elections when Kwasniewski won, has not given up reminding the government of the need for tough budget policies.
Belka has defended the budget deficit, which is forecast to be 2.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year.
This is under the three percent target western European countries must achieve to join economic and monetary union (EMU), a target laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.

But Gronkiewicz-Waltz indicated that meeting Maastricht was not enough for Poland. "This year is 2.8 percent. In my opinion this is extremely high. This is below the Maastricht criterion but last year it was 2.4," she said.
"(Belka) should be very disciplined this year and next year," she said. "I would like to have 2.2 percent but I don't know if that's possible."
She also ruled out early interest rates cuts, even though rates are now about five percentage points over inflation, due to a surge in corporate and consumer lending by banks.
"Interest rates depend on inflation and credit growth. Both are too high now," she said.
"I don't think that we could cut interest rates soon. This I can exclude," she said. "But you can never know what will happen in two or three months. In our case that's quite long-term."
